note:
Postpartum day 2 progress note for a 30-year-old female, gravida 2 para 2, who delivered a healthy term infant vaginally two days ago. Her labor was uncomplicated, but she sustained a second-degree perineal laceration that was repaired at delivery, and the estimated blood loss was 450 mL.

This morning she reports moderate perineal pain, about 4 out of 10, which is improving with medication. Her bleeding is lighter than yesterday. She is breastfeeding and says the baby is latching better since the lactation nurse visited. She feels tired and a little lightheaded when she stands up quickly. She denies chest pain, shortness of breath, fever, calf pain, and heavy vaginal bleeding. She has not had headaches or visual changes. She has not had a bowel movement since delivery and is worried about straining over her stitches.

She has no known drug allergies. For medications, she takes ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours as prescribed on the unit. She also uses over-the-counter supplements: a prenatal multivitamin daily, and fenugreek capsules that she started two days ago hoping to increase her milk supply. She took ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily during pregnancy for mild anemia but has not taken it since admission.

On examination she is tired-appearing but comfortable. Temperature is 98.4 F, heart rate 92, blood pressure 108/66, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. The fundus is firm at the umbilicus and nontender. Lochia is moderate rubra without clots. The perineal repair is intact with mild edema and no hematoma or purulent drainage. Her breasts are soft. Her calves are soft and nontender without swelling. Lungs are clear and heart rhythm is regular. Hemoglobin this morning is 9.8 g/dL, down from 11.2 g/dL before delivery, and the platelet count is normal.

My impression is postpartum day 2 after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery with a second-degree perineal laceration, mild postpartum anemia from blood loss, and a risk of constipation. Her lightheadedness is most consistent with the anemia and should improve with iron. We will continue ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours with food, and she may use ice packs and sitz baths for perineal comfort. I am starting docusate 100 mg twice daily to prevent constipation and restarting ferrous sulfate 325 mg once daily. She should continue her prenatal multivitamin daily. I advised her to stop the fenugreek capsules and to review her milk supply concerns with the lactation nurse instead, because it can upset the stomach and its benefit is unproven. A repeat hemoglobin will be checked tomorrow morning, and she is expected to go home tomorrow with a postpartum clinic visit in two weeks.
summary: A 30-year-old female on postpartum day 2 after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery was seen on the ward. She had a second-degree perineal laceration with an estimated blood loss of 450 mL and reports improving perineal pain, tiredness, and lightheadedness on standing, while denying chest pain, fever, calf pain, and heavy vaginal bleeding. Hemoglobin was 9.8 g/dL, down from 11.2 g/dL before delivery, with an intact perineal repair and a firm fundus. The clinician assessed mild postpartum anemia and a risk of constipation. The plan is to continue ibuprofen, start docusate, restart ferrous sulfate, stop fenugreek capsules, repeat hemoglobin tomorrow, and arrange postpartum clinic follow-up.

No bowel movement since delivery. Denies chest pain, shortness of breath, fever, calf pain, heavy vaginal bleeding, headaches, and visual changes. No known drug allergies. Takes ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours, a prenatal multivitamin daily, and fenugreek capsules started two days ago; took ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily during pregnancy for mild anemia but not since admission.

Fundus firm at the umbilicus and nontender; moderate rubra lochia without clots. Perineal repair intact with mild edema, no hematoma or purulent drainage. Breasts soft; calves soft and nontender without swelling; lungs clear; regular heart rhythm. Hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL (11.2 g/dL before delivery); platelet count normal.
soap.assessment: Postpartum day 2 after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery with a second-degree perineal laceration; mild postpartum anemia from blood loss with associated lightheadedness; risk of constipation.
plan: Continue ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours with food
Ice packs and sitz baths for perineal comfort
Start docusate 100 mg twice daily to prevent constipation
Restart ferrous sulfate 325 mg once daily
Continue prenatal multivitamin daily
Stop fenugreek capsules and review milk supply concerns with the lactation nurse
Repeat hemoglobin tomorrow morning
Expected discharge tomorrow with postpartum clinic visit in two weeks

note:
Dictating a dermatology clinic follow-up visit for a 25-year-old male with hidradenitis suppurativa. He is here because of worsening painful nodules in both armpits and in the groin, which he has had for about four years, and he says the flares now come every two to three weeks with drainage that stains his shirts. He rates the pain at seven out of ten during a flare. He denies fever, chills, weight loss, joint pain, abdominal pain, and diarrhea, and he has had no hospital stays. He is a smoker, about half a pack a day.

He is very anxious today and asked me a lot of questions, so I will list them. He asked whether this is contagious and I told him it is not. He asked whether poor hygiene caused it and I told him no. He asked whether shaving or deodorant is to blame, whether his diet matters, whether it will scar, whether the biologic can cause cancer or serious infection, whether he can drink alcohol on treatment, and whether he will have this forever. I answered each one in plain language, went over the expected course, and gave him a written handout.

For current treatment, he tells me he takes doxycycline 50 mg twice daily, correction, that is 100 mg twice daily, which I confirmed from his pharmacy list, and he has been on it for about four months with only partial improvement. He uses clindamycin 1% topical solution once daily on the armpits and groin and washes with chlorhexidine in the shower. For pain he takes acetaminophen 500 mg every six hours as needed. He also takes over-the-counter supplements on his own, namely zinc gluconate 50 mg daily, turmeric capsules, and vitamin D3 2000 units daily, and he wanted to know if these are helping. He has no known drug allergies.

On examination, blood pressure 126/78, heart rate 84, temperature 98.6 F, weight 98 kilograms, body mass index 31. Skin examination shows multiple inflamed nodules, two draining sinus tracts, and scarring in the left axilla, with similar findings in the right axilla and both inguinal folds, consistent with Hurley stage two. There is one tender fluctuant abscess about 2 cm in the left axilla. There is no spreading redness and no enlarged lymph nodes. I performed an incision and drainage of the left axillary abscess under 1% lidocaine local anesthesia, with a moderate amount of pus released, and he tolerated it well despite his nervousness.

My impression is hidradenitis suppurativa, Hurley stage two, with an inadequate response to doxycycline and a left axillary abscess drained today. For the plan, I am stopping the doxycycline. I am increasing the clindamycin 1% solution to twice daily. I ordered QuantiFERON, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibody, a complete blood count, and a comprehensive metabolic panel, and once these return normal I will start adalimumab, 160 mg subcutaneously on day one, 80 mg on day fifteen, then 40 mg weekly. He will continue the chlorhexidine wash and acetaminophen as needed. I told him the evidence for turmeric is weak, but he may continue zinc gluconate and vitamin D3 if he wishes. I counseled him on smoking cessation and weight loss and placed a dietitian referral. Injection teaching will be done by our nurse. He should return in four weeks, or sooner for fever, spreading redness, or a new painful lump that does not drain. End of dictation.
summary: A 25-year-old male with hidradenitis suppurativa presented with worsening painful nodules and drainage in both armpits and the groin, with flares every two to three weeks despite four months of doxycycline. He was very anxious and asked many questions, and he takes zinc gluconate, turmeric capsules, and vitamin D3 on his own. Examination showed Hurley stage two disease with a fluctuant left axillary abscess, which was incised and drained. The assessment was hidradenitis suppurativa with inadequate response to doxycycline. Doxycycline was stopped, clindamycin was increased to twice daily, screening tests were ordered before starting adalimumab, and follow-up is in four weeks.

Multiple inflamed nodules, two draining sinus tracts, and scarring in the left axilla, with similar findings in the right axilla and both inguinal folds, consistent with Hurley stage two. One tender fluctuant abscess about 2 cm in the left axilla. No spreading redness or enlarged lymph nodes. Incision and drainage of the left axillary abscess under 1% lidocaine was performed with moderate pus released.
soap.assessment: Hidradenitis suppurativa, Hurley stage two, with inadequate response to doxycycline; left axillary abscess drained today.
plan: Stop doxycycline
Increase clindamycin 1% solution to twice daily
Order QuantiFERON, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibody, complete blood count, and comprehensive metabolic panel
Start adalimumab 160 mg subcutaneously on day one, 80 mg on day fifteen, then 40 mg weekly once screening results are normal
Continue chlorhexidine wash and acetaminophen as needed
May continue zinc gluconate and vitamin D3; evidence for turmeric is weak
Smoking cessation and weight loss counseling with dietitian referral
Nurse injection teaching
Return in four weeks, or sooner for fever, spreading redness, or a new painful lump that does not drain

note:
Doctor: Good morning. I understand we have a 10-year-old male here with a sore throat. What has been going on?
Family member: He started complaining of a sore throat two days ago, and last night he felt really hot. I checked and it was 101.8.
Patient: It hurts when I swallow. And my head hurts too.
Doctor: Any cough or runny nose?
Family member: No, nothing like that.
Patient: My tummy hurt a little yesterday, but I didn't throw up.
Doctor: Okay. Any rash, or trouble breathing?
Family member: No rash, and he is breathing fine.
Doctor: Is anyone sick at home or at school?
Family member: A couple of kids in his class had strep throat last week.
Doctor: Does he have any medical conditions?
Family member: He has mild asthma. He uses his albuterol inhaler, two puffs, only when he is wheezy, which has not happened in months. And he takes cetirizine 10 mg every day for his seasonal allergies.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?
Family member: No, none.
Doctor: Great. His temperature today is 101.2, heart rate 104, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. His weight is 32 kilograms. Let me look in the throat. Open wide and say ahh. His tonsils are red and swollen with white patches, and I feel tender, swollen glands in the front of his neck. His ears look normal, his lungs are clear with no wheezing, and there is no rash. We did a rapid strep test and it came back positive.
Family member: So it is strep?
Doctor: Yes. This is streptococcal pharyngitis. His asthma and allergies are well controlled, so no changes there. I am starting amoxicillin 1000 mg once daily for 10 days. It is important to finish all of it, even when he feels better. For the fever and throat pain he can have ibuprofen 200 mg every six hours as needed with food. Lots of fluids and soft foods are fine. He should stay home from school until he has had 24 hours of antibiotics and has no fever. Please throw away his toothbrush and get a new one after two days of treatment.
Family member: What should we watch for?
Doctor: Come back if he cannot swallow liquids, starts drooling, has trouble breathing, gets a rash, or the fever lasts more than 48 hours after starting the medicine. Otherwise no routine recheck is needed.
Family member: Okay, thank you.
summary: A 10-year-old male presented with two days of sore throat, fever up to 101.8, headache, and mild abdominal discomfort, with no cough, runny nose, or rash. He has mild asthma and seasonal allergies that are well controlled. Examination showed red swollen tonsils with white patches and tender anterior neck glands, and a rapid strep test was positive. The assessment was streptococcal pharyngitis. He was started on amoxicillin for 10 days with ibuprofen as needed, advised to stay home until 24 hours of antibiotics and no fever, and given return precautions.

soap.subjective: 10-year-old male with two days of sore throat, pain on swallowing, fever (101.8 at home), headache, and mild abdominal discomfort the previous day without vomiting. No cough, runny nose, rash, or trouble breathing. Classmates recently had strep throat. History of mild asthma (albuterol two puffs only when wheezy, none in months) and seasonal allergies on cetirizine 10 mg every day. No medication allergies.
soap.objective: Temperature 101.2, heart rate 104, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, weight 32 kilograms. Tonsils red and swollen with white patches; tender swollen anterior cervical glands. Ears normal, lungs clear without wheezing, no rash. Rapid strep test positive.
soap.assessment: Streptococcal pharyngitis. Asthma and seasonal allergies well controlled.
plan: Start amoxicillin 1000 mg once daily for 10 days and complete the full course
Ibuprofen 200 mg every six hours as needed with food for fever and throat pain
Fluids and soft foods
Stay home from school until 24 hours of antibiotics and no fever
Replace toothbrush after two days of treatment
Continue albuterol as needed and cetirizine 10 mg every day without changes
Return if unable to swallow liquids, drooling, trouble breathing, rash, or fever lasting more than 48 hours after starting treatment

note:
Telehealth video visit note, geriatrics. The patient is an 86-year-old male seen by secure video from his home, with his daughter beside him to help with the camera and read his medication bottles. He consented to the video format and confirmed his location.

The reason for the visit is follow-up of osteoporosis after a fragility fracture. Three months ago he developed sudden mid-back pain after bending to lift a laundry basket, and a lateral spine x-ray showed an L1 compression fracture. A DXA scan last month showed a T-score of -2.9 at the femoral neck. He has not yet started any bone-protective medication. His back pain is now 3 out of 10 at rest and 5 out of 10 after standing for a long time. He denies new back pain, numbness, leg weakness, or bowel or bladder changes. He has had no falls.

He returned 9 days ago from a 14-hour international flight to visit relatives overseas. During the trip he skipped some doses of his medicines and drank little water. Since returning he denies calf pain, leg swelling, chest pain, shortness of breath, fever, and diarrhea. He feels tired from jet lag but is otherwise well.

He is allergic to ibuprofen and other NSAIDs, which cause hives, so NSAIDs are avoided. His history includes hypertension, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and stage 3a chronic kidney disease. His medications are amlodipine 5 mg daily, tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily, calcium carbonate 500 mg twice daily with meals, and a vitamin D supplement. He first said he takes vitamin D 5000 units daily, but his daughter read the bottle on camera and corrected this to vitamin D3 1000 units daily. After the fracture, an urgent care physician prescribed tramadol 50 mg every 6 hours as needed. He took it for two weeks and then stopped on his own because of dizziness and constipation. For pain he now uses acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed.

Home measurements today were blood pressure 128/74, pulse 72, and temperature 98.2 F. His weight is stable at 71 kilograms according to his daughter. Labs drawn before the visit showed creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, eGFR 52, calcium 9.4 mg/dL, and 25-hydroxy vitamin D 24 ng/mL.

On video examination he appears comfortable and speaks in full sentences. There is mild thoracic kyphosis. He stood and walked a few steps with his walker, and his gait was slow but steady. He held both legs up to the camera and there was no visible swelling, redness, or asymmetry.

My assessment is osteoporosis with a recent L1 compression fragility fracture and high fracture risk, vitamin D insufficiency, and stage 3a chronic kidney disease with an eGFR of 52, which still allows an oral bisphosphonate. Suspicion for venous thromboembolism after the long flight is low because he has no symptoms and no leg findings.

For the plan, I am starting alendronate 70 mg once weekly, to be taken in the morning on an empty stomach with a full glass of water, and he must stay upright for 30 minutes afterward. He will continue calcium carbonate 500 mg twice daily with meals. I am increasing vitamin D3 from 1000 units to 2000 units daily. He will continue acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed, and tramadol remains discontinued. NSAIDs stay off his list. I ordered a basic metabolic panel and a repeat 25-hydroxy vitamin D level in three months. I placed a referral to physical therapy for balance and back strengthening, and we reviewed fall precautions. He and his daughter know to seek care promptly for calf pain, leg swelling, chest pain, or new severe back pain. Follow-up will be a video visit in six weeks.
summary: An 86-year-old male was seen by video for osteoporosis after an L1 compression fracture, with a femoral neck T-score of -2.9 and mild residual back pain. He returned nine days earlier from a long international flight and denies calf pain, leg swelling, chest pain, or shortness of breath. He is allergic to NSAIDs and stopped tramadol on his own because of dizziness and constipation. The assessment was osteoporosis with a recent fragility fracture, vitamin D insufficiency, and stage 3a chronic kidney disease. Alendronate weekly was started, vitamin D3 was increased to 2000 units daily, acetaminophen continues, and physical therapy and a six-week video follow-up were arranged.

soap.subjective: 86-year-old male with osteoporosis after an L1 compression fragility fracture three months ago from bending to lift a laundry basket. Back pain 3 out of 10 at rest and 5 out of 10 after prolonged standing; denies new back pain, numbness, leg weakness, bowel or bladder changes, and falls. Returned 9 days ago from a 14-hour international flight with some skipped medication doses and low fluid intake; denies calf pain, leg swelling, chest pain, shortness of breath, fever, and diarrhea; tired from jet lag. soap.objective: Home blood pressure 128/74, pulse 72, temperature 98.2 F, weight 71 kilograms (stable). Lateral spine x-ray showed an L1 compression fracture; DXA T-score -2.9 at the femoral neck. Labs: creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, eGFR 52, calcium 9.4 mg/dL, 25-hydroxy vitamin D 24 ng/mL. Video exam: comfortable, speaks in full sentences, mild thoracic kyphosis, slow but steady gait with walker, no visible leg swelling, redness, or asymmetry.
soap.assessment: Osteoporosis with a recent L1 compression fragility fracture and high fracture risk; vitamin D insufficiency; stage 3a chronic kidney disease with eGFR 52 that allows an oral bisphosphonate; low suspicion for venous thromboembolism after the long flight.
plan: Start alendronate 70 mg once weekly in the morning on an empty stomach with a full glass of water, upright for 30 minutes
Continue calcium carbonate 500 mg twice daily with meals
Increase vitamin D3 from 1000 units to 2000 units daily
Continue acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed; tramadol remains discontinued; avoid NSAIDs
Order basic metabolic panel and repeat 25-hydroxy vitamin D in three months
Refer to physical therapy for balance and back strengthening; review fall precautions
Seek care promptly for calf pain, leg swelling, chest pain, or new severe back pain
Follow-up video visit in six weeks

note:
Hospital day 3 dermatology progress note for a 66-year-old female with moderate plaque psoriasis on a biologic who was admitted with cellulitis of the right lower leg. Her psoriasis has been followed for about 12 years and has been controlled on secukinumab 300 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks, with her last dose 2 weeks before admission. Her other history includes type 2 diabetes.

There were no events overnight. She says the right leg is less painful and less red than on admission. Over the past week the plaques on her elbows, knees, and scalp have become more scaly and itchy, which she attributes to the stress of being in the hospital. She denies fever, chills, joint pain, new pustules, diarrhea, and mouth sores. She has no known drug allergies.

Her current medications are cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours and metformin 500 mg twice daily. Her secukinumab has been on hold since admission because of the active infection.

Vital signs this morning were temperature 99.1 F, heart rate 82, blood pressure 132/76, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. On examination, the redness on the right shin has receded about 2 cm from the marked border, with mild warmth and trace tenderness and no fluctuance or purulent drainage. Well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale are present on both elbows, both knees, and the scalp, covering about 8% of her body surface area. There are no pustules and no swollen joints. White blood cell count is 9.4, down from 13.2 on admission. Blood cultures from admission show no growth at 48 hours. Her QuantiFERON test before starting the biologic was negative according to her chart. Glucose this morning was 148 mg/dL.

My impression is right lower leg cellulitis that is improving on intravenous antibiotics, and moderate plaque psoriasis with a mild flare while secukinumab is on hold. Her diabetes is stable. I will continue cefazolin today and, if she stays afebrile, switch to oral cephalexin 500 mg four times daily tomorrow to complete a 7-day course. Secukinumab will remain on hold until the cellulitis has resolved, and then she may resume it at her next scheduled dose. I am starting clobetasol 0.05% ointment twice daily to the plaques on her elbows and knees for 2 weeks, avoiding the right leg, the face, and skin folds, along with a thick emollient after bathing. Metformin continues unchanged. She will follow up in the dermatology clinic in 4 weeks.
summary: A 66-year-old female with moderate plaque psoriasis on secukinumab was seen on hospital day 3 of an admission for right lower leg cellulitis. Her plaques on the elbows, knees, and scalp have become more scaly and itchy, and she denies fever, joint pain, new pustules, and diarrhea. The cellulitis is improving, her white blood cell count fell from 13.2 to 9.4, and plaques cover about 8% of her body surface area. The assessment was improving cellulitis and a mild psoriasis flare while the biologic is held. Plan is to switch to oral cephalexin tomorrow, keep secukinumab on hold, start clobetasol ointment, and arrange clinic follow-up in 4 weeks.

No events overnight. Right leg less painful and less red. Elbow, knee, and scalp plaques more scaly and itchy over the past week. Denies fever, chills, joint pain, new pustules, diarrhea, and mouth sores. No known drug allergies. Current medications cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours and metformin 500 mg twice daily; secukinumab on hold since admission.

Keep secukinumab on hold until the cellulitis resolves, then resume at the next scheduled dose

note:
Doctor: Hello. I see we have a 7-month-old male here for a cough and fast breathing. Tell me what has been going on.
Family member: He has had a runny nose for about four days, and for the last two days he has a bad cough and he breathes fast. He is wheezing a little at night.
Doctor: Any fever?
Family member: No fever. I checked a few times and the highest was 99.
Doctor: Any vomiting? Has he turned blue or stopped breathing at any point?
Family member: No vomiting, and no, nothing like that. He is eating less though, about half of his usual bottles, but he still has wet diapers. Four or five today.
Doctor: Good. Does he have any medical problems, or take any medicines?
Family member: No, he was born at term and has been healthy. No medicines.
Doctor: Okay, let me examine him. His respiratory rate is 48, oxygen saturation is 97% on room air, and temperature is 99.2. He is alert and playful. I hear scattered wheezes and crackles in both lungs, with mild nasal flaring but no chest retractions. His ears and throat look normal and he is well hydrated. This is bronchiolitis, a viral infection of the small airways. Antibiotics and inhalers do not help this, so we treat the symptoms. Use saline nose drops, then gently suction his nose before feeds. Offer smaller, more frequent feedings. Go to the emergency room if he breathes very fast or hard, his lips look blue, he has fewer than three wet diapers in a day, or he takes less than half of his feeds.
Family member: How long will this last?
Doctor: The cough can last two to three weeks, and the worst days are usually days three to five. I would like to recheck him in two days.
Family member: Okay, thank you.
summary: A 7-month-old male presented with four days of runny nose and two days of cough, fast breathing, and nighttime wheezing, eating about half his usual bottles but still having wet diapers. There was no fever, vomiting, or color change. Examination showed a respiratory rate of 48, oxygen saturation of 97% on room air, and scattered wheezes and crackles with mild nasal flaring and no retractions. The assessment was bronchiolitis. Treatment is supportive with saline nose drops and gentle nasal suction before feeds, smaller more frequent feedings, return precautions, and a recheck in two days.

soap.subjective: 7-month-old male, born at term and healthy, with a runny nose for about four days and for two days a bad cough, fast breathing, and mild wheezing at night. Eating about half of his usual bottles but still has four or five wet diapers today. No fever (highest 99), vomiting, color change, or pauses in breathing. No medical problems or medicines.
soap.objective: Respiratory rate 48, oxygen saturation 97% on room air, temperature 99.2. Alert and playful, well hydrated. Scattered wheezes and crackles in both lungs with mild nasal flaring, no chest retractions. Ears and throat normal.
soap.assessment: Bronchiolitis, a viral infection of the small airways.
plan: Saline nose drops followed by gentle nasal suction before feeds
Offer smaller, more frequent feedings
No antibiotics or inhalers; symptomatic treatment only
Go to the emergency room for very fast or hard breathing, blue lips, fewer than three wet diapers in a day, or taking less than half of feeds
Recheck in two days

note:
Geriatrics ward progress note for a 71-year-old female admitted for evaluation of frailty and unintentional weight loss. She has lost about 8 kg over the past 4 months, from 57 kg to 49 kg, with a poor appetite. She lives alone in a rural area, no longer drives, and depends on a neighbor for rides, which has caused her to miss two clinic appointments. She says she feels weak and tired and has trouble climbing stairs. She denies trouble swallowing, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, blood in the stool, fever, and night sweats. Her only chronic problem is hypertension, treated with amlodipine 5 mg daily. She has no known drug allergies.

Vital signs this morning were blood pressure 118/70, heart rate 76, and temperature 98.2 F, with a weight of 49 kg and a body mass index of 19. She looks thin with temporal wasting but is alert and oriented. Her abdomen is soft and nontender without masses. Labs show albumin 3.1 g/dL, hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, TSH 2.3, and creatinine 0.8 mg/dL. A chest x-ray was clear.

My impression is frailty with unintentional weight loss, most likely from poor oral intake and social factors, with no red flags for malignancy on the initial workup. I am starting an oral nutritional supplement twice daily between meals and continuing amlodipine 5 mg daily. Dietitian and social work consults are placed. Social work will arrange non-emergency medical transport vouchers and home-delivered meals, because transportation is the main barrier to follow-up. I will call her by telephone one week after discharge, and her geriatrics clinic visit in 4 weeks will be scheduled with a ride arranged in advance.
summary: A 71-year-old female admitted to the geriatrics ward has lost about 8 kg over 4 months with poor appetite, weakness, and fatigue. She denies trouble swallowing, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, fever, and night sweats, and she lives alone in a rural area where transportation has caused missed appointments. Her weight is 49 kg, albumin is 3.1 g/dL, and a chest x-ray was clear. The assessment was frailty with unintentional weight loss from poor oral intake and social factors. Plan is an oral nutritional supplement, dietitian and social work consults for transport and meals, and telephone follow-up one week after discharge.

soap.subjective: 71-year-old female admitted for frailty and unintentional weight loss of about 8 kg over 4 months (57 kg to 49 kg) with poor appetite, weakness, tiredness, and trouble climbing stairs. note:

HPI: pt c/o urinary incontinence x ~6 mo, worse past 2 wks. Sudden urge, leaks before reaching toilet, 4-5 pads/day. Nocturia x3. Denies dysuria, hematuria, fever, flank pain. No stool incontinence. Takes diphenhydramine 25 mg qHS OTC for sleep + cranberry capsules daily "for the bladder".
PMH: HTN, OA, chronic LE edema
Meds: amlodipine 5 mg daily, furosemide 20 mg qPM, diphenhydramine 25 mg qHS (OTC), cranberry capsules daily (OTC)
NKDA

Vitals: BP 138/72, HR 70, T 98.0 F, RR 16, SpO2 96% RA
Exam: pleasant, A&O x3, NAD
 abd soft, NT, no suprapubic fullness
 atrophic vaginal mucosa, no prolapse, perineal skin intact no rash
 trace LE edema bilat
 gait slow w/ walker
Data: PVR by bladder scan 40 mL. UA neg nitrite, neg LE, no blood. Na 139, K 4.0, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, glucose 98.

To do:
- d/c diphenhydramine (anticholinergic)
- move furosemide 20 mg to qAM
- start estradiol 0.01% vaginal cream 0.5 g twice weekly
- timed voiding q2h while awake, bedside commode at night
- cut evening fluids + caffeine
- cranberry caps no proven benefit, ok to continue if pt wishes
- PT eval for gait/mobility
- f/u geri clinic 4 wks, recheck sx

The assessment was urge incontinence worsened by diphenhydramine, evening furosemide, and vaginal atrophy, without UTI or retention. Diphenhydramine was stopped, furosemide moved to the morning, vaginal estradiol cream started, and timed voiding and PT were arranged.

Hx: ischemic cardiomyopathy, EF 30% on echo 4 mo ago. CAD s/p MI + PCI. HTN, HLD, knee OA.

- low Na diet, mostly adherent; wife helps w/ meds

Meds per pt: carvedilol 6.25 mg BID -- correction, wife's pill list shows carvedilol 12.5 mg BID (bottle confirmed). Losartan 50 mg daily. Spironolactone 25 mg daily. Furosemide 40 mg daily. Dapagliflozin 10 mg daily. Atorvastatin 40 mg qHS. ASA 81 mg daily. Diltiazem ER 120 mg daily (urgent care). Ibuprofen PRN.

Vitals: BP 118/72, HR 64, RR 16, SpO2 97% RA, wt 84.6 kg (86.4 kg 3 mo ago). No orthostatic drop.
Exam: JVP ~6 cm, no HJR. Lungs clear. RRR, no S3, no murmur. Abd soft. No LE edema. Extremities warm.

- d/c ibuprofen, use acetaminophen 500 mg PRN for knee pain (max 3 g/day)

- f/u 4 wks

note:
Geriatrics memory clinic follow-up note for a 69-year-old female seen for mild cognitive impairment. She was referred by her primary care physician because of about 18 months of gradual forgetfulness. She misplaces items, repeats questions, and has trouble recalling names, and she says this is worse when she is tired. Her husband attended the visit, confirms the history, and describes no sudden change. She remains independent in all basic activities and manages her own medications with a weekly pillbox, although she now relies on a calendar for appointments. She denies getting lost while driving, hallucinations, falls, personality change, focal weakness, and head injury. Her mood is good, but she sleeps poorly and has been taking over-the-counter diphenhydramine 25 mg at bedtime.

Her history includes hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Her medications are lisinopril 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and the diphenhydramine. She has no known drug allergies.

On examination, blood pressure is 134/80 and heart rate is 72. She is alert and oriented to person, place, and time, with fluent speech and intact cranial nerves. Strength, tone, and reflexes are normal, there is no tremor, and her gait is normal. Her MoCA score is 23 out of 30, with points lost on delayed recall and on visuospatial and executive items. Her PHQ-9 score is 4. B12 is 245 pg/mL, TSH is 2.1, and her CBC and CMP are normal. An MRI brain from last month shows mild generalized atrophy and mild chronic small-vessel changes without stroke, mass, or hydrocephalus.

My impression is amnestic mild cognitive impairment, without dementia because her daily function is preserved. Contributing factors are poor sleep, a low-normal B12, and the anticholinergic effect of diphenhydramine. I am stopping the diphenhydramine and reviewed sleep hygiene measures with her. I am starting cyanocobalamin 1000 mcg daily. She will continue lisinopril and atorvastatin, and we discussed keeping her blood pressure well controlled. I explained that a cholinesterase inhibitor has no proven benefit in mild cognitive impairment, so I am not prescribing one. I encouraged regular aerobic exercise and a Mediterranean-style diet and referred her for neuropsychological testing. I will repeat the MoCA in 6 months, and she is fine to keep driving for now.

MoCA was 23 out of 30, B12 was 245 pg/mL, and MRI brain showed mild atrophy and small-vessel changes without stroke or mass. The assessment was amnestic mild cognitive impairment. Diphenhydramine was stopped, cyanocobalamin was started, neuropsychological testing was ordered, and the MoCA will be repeated in 6 months.

note:
Doctor: Good afternoon. I have you down as a 29-year-old male here for recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection. Can you walk me through what has happened?
Patient: Yeah, this is the third time. The first was about six months ago. I had a tooth abscess and got amoxicillin-clavulanate, and a week after I finished I had awful watery diarrhea.
Doctor: How was that treated?
Patient: Oral vancomycin, I think 250 milligrams four times a day for ten days.
Doctor: The pharmacy record I have says 125 milligrams four times a day. Does that sound right?
Patient: Oh, okay, yeah, 125. That sounds right. It went away, and then it came back about two months later.
Doctor: And then?
Patient: They gave me fidaxomicin, the 200 milligram pills twice a day for ten days. I was fine for almost three months, and then four days ago the watery diarrhea started again. Five or six times a day, with cramps, and I felt feverish.
Doctor: Any blood in the stool? Any vomiting?
Patient: No blood, no vomiting.
Doctor: Any antibiotics since the fidaxomicin?
Patient: No, nothing.
Doctor: What other medicines do you take?
Patient: Omeprazole 20 milligrams every day for heartburn, and sertraline 50 milligrams daily for anxiety. And I have been taking loperamide, like four tablets a day, to stop the diarrhea.
Doctor: Okay. How much alcohol do you drink?
Patient: Honestly, a lot. Probably eight to ten beers a day, more on my days off. I get shaky in the morning if I do not drink.
Doctor: Thank you for telling me. That counts as heavy alcohol use, and it matters for your treatment. What do you do for work?
Patient: I work rotating shifts at a warehouse, nights one week and days the next, so my meals and sleep are all over the place.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Your temperature is 99.8, heart rate 98, and blood pressure 118/74. Your mouth is a little dry, and your belly is tender in the lower part, but there is no rebound or guarding and it is not swollen. The stool C. difficile toxin from urgent care was positive. Your labs today show a white blood cell count of 12.4, creatinine 0.9, and albumin 3.6.
Patient: So is it bad?
Doctor: This is your third episode, so this is recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection. It is not severe, because your white count is under 15 and your kidneys are fine. Your acid reducer and the alcohol both raise the risk of it coming back. Here is the plan. I am restarting oral vancomycin 125 milligrams four times daily for 10 days, then tapering to twice daily for a week, once daily for a week, and every other day for two weeks. Space the doses over the hours you are awake, and set phone alarms around your shift changes. Stop the omeprazole, because acid suppression makes this worse, and start famotidine 20 milligrams at bedtime for the heartburn, which is reflux disease. Stop the loperamide, as it can trap the toxin. I am referring you for a fecal microbiota transplant, since this is your third recurrence.
Patient: And the drinking?
Doctor: Stopping suddenly can be dangerous at your level of drinking, so please do not quit cold. I am starting thiamine 100 milligrams daily and referring you to addiction medicine to plan a supervised reduction. Continue sertraline as is. Go to the emergency room for bloody stools, severe belly pain, a swollen belly, or a high fever, and I will see you in two weeks.
Patient: Okay, I will try.
summary: A 29-year-old male shift worker with heavy alcohol use presented with his third episode of Clostridioides difficile infection, with four days of watery diarrhea, cramps, and feeling feverish, and no blood in the stool or vomiting. He had been taking omeprazole and loperamide, and he first misremembered his prior vancomycin dose, which was corrected to 125 mg. Stool toxin was positive, white blood cell count was 12.4, and creatinine was 0.9. The assessment was non-severe recurrent infection. Vancomycin was restarted with a taper, omeprazole and loperamide were stopped, famotidine and thiamine were started, and referrals were made for fecal microbiota transplant and addiction medicine.

soap.subjective: 29-year-old male with a third episode of Clostridioides difficile infection. First episode about six months ago after amoxicillin-clavulanate for a tooth abscess, treated with oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days (patient first said 250 mg, corrected against the pharmacy record); recurred about two months later and was treated with fidaxomicin 200 mg twice daily for 10 days. Four days of watery diarrhea five or six times a day, cramps, and feeling feverish. No blood in the stool, no vomiting, no recent antibiotics. Takes omeprazole 20 mg daily for heartburn, sertraline 50 mg daily for anxiety, and has been taking loperamide about four tablets a day. Heavy alcohol use, eight to ten beers a day, with morning shakiness when not drinking. Works rotating night and day shifts at a warehouse. No medication allergies.
soap.objective: Temperature 99.8, heart rate 98, blood pressure 118/74. Mildly dry mouth, lower abdominal tenderness without rebound, guarding, or distension. Stool C. difficile toxin positive. White blood cell count 12.4, creatinine 0.9, albumin 3.6.
soap.assessment: Third episode of recurrent non-severe Clostridioides difficile infection (white count under 15, normal kidney function), with acid suppression and alcohol as risk factors; heartburn from reflux disease; heavy alcohol use; anxiety.
plan: Restart oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days, then taper to twice daily for a week, once daily for a week, and every other day for two weeks
Space doses over waking hours and set phone alarms around shift changes
Stop omeprazole and start famotidine 20 mg at bedtime
Stop loperamide
Refer for fecal microbiota transplant
Start thiamine 100 mg daily and refer to addiction medicine for supervised alcohol reduction; do not stop drinking abruptly
Continue sertraline
Emergency room for bloody stools, severe or swollen belly, or high fever
Follow-up in two weeks

note:
Preventive care progress note for a 44-year-old female on the hospital medical ward, where she has been under overnight observation for dehydration from viral gastroenteritis. She is medically ready for discharge this afternoon, and because she is due for her annual preventive review, we completed it before she leaves.

Her gastroenteritis has resolved. She denies nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain since last night and is eating normally. She also denies chest pain, shortness of breath, and headaches. She has hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine 75 mcg daily and no other chronic conditions. She has no known drug allergies. She does not smoke, drinks alcohol rarely, walks three times a week, and sleeps about seven hours a night. Her last Pap smear was two years ago and was normal with a negative HPV test. She has never had a screening mammogram. Her last tetanus booster was about 12 years ago, she has not had an influenza vaccine this season, and her last COVID-19 vaccine dose was more than a year ago. She has never had a serious reaction to a vaccine.

Vital signs this morning were blood pressure 118/74, heart rate 70, temperature 98.2 F, respiratory rate 14, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Her weight is 72 kg with a body mass index of 27. She is well appearing with moist mucous membranes. Her heart rhythm is regular without a murmur, her lungs are clear, her abdomen is soft and nontender, her thyroid is not enlarged, and she has no leg edema. Her creatinine this morning was 0.8 mg/dL with a normal sodium and potassium. Her TSH last month in clinic was 6.8.

My impression is that she is due for annual preventive care and vaccine updates, her hypothyroidism is not optimally controlled, and her viral gastroenteritis and dehydration have resolved. She received the influenza vaccine 0.5 mL intramuscularly and the Tdap vaccine 0.5 mL intramuscularly on the ward today and tolerated both without any immediate reaction. We discussed an updated COVID-19 vaccine, but she prefers to wait and will revisit this at her clinic visit. I am increasing levothyroxine from 75 mcg to 88 mcg daily and will repeat a TSH in 6 to 8 weeks. I ordered a screening mammogram, and a lipid panel and hemoglobin A1c were added to this morning's blood draw. Her next Pap smear is due in three years, and we talked about starting colorectal cancer screening next year at age 45. She will follow up with her primary care clinic in 6 to 8 weeks.

note:
Dictating an orthopedic clinic visit for a 52-year-old male with a left ankle injury. He works rotating twelve-hour shifts with an irregular schedule, and five days ago, at the end of a night shift, he rolled his left ankle stepping off a curb. He felt a pop, had immediate lateral ankle pain and swelling, and was able to walk afterward with a limp. Bruising has developed along the outside of the ankle. Pain is 6 out of 10 with walking and 2 out of 10 at rest. He denies numbness, tingling, knee pain, and calf pain, and he has no history of injury to this ankle.

His history includes paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. He tells me he takes apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, correction, 5 mg twice daily, which I confirmed from a photo of his pill bottle on his phone. He also takes metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily and atorvastatin 40 mg daily. For the last four days he has been taking over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day for the ankle, plus acetaminophen 500 mg as needed. Because his shifts rotate, he admits his apixaban doses are sometimes spaced unevenly, so we talked about anchoring the doses to when he wakes and when he goes to bed regardless of the shift. He has no known drug allergies.

On examination, blood pressure is 132/80 and heart rate is 68. The left ankle has swelling and ecchymosis over the lateral malleolus and the front of the ankle. He is tender over the anterior talofibular ligament. There is no tenderness over the posterior edge or tip of the lateral malleolus, the medial malleolus, the navicular, or the base of the fifth metatarsal, and the squeeze test is negative. The anterior drawer is mildly positive with a soft endpoint, and the talar tilt is stable. He took four steps in the exam room with a limp. Sensation is intact and the dorsalis pedis pulse is palpable with brisk capillary refill. The calf is soft and nontender. An x-ray of the left ankle with three views shows no fracture, mild lateral soft tissue swelling, and an intact ankle mortise. His labs from cardiology last month showed hemoglobin 14.2 g/dL and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL.

My impression is a grade 2 lateral ankle sprain involving the anterior talofibular ligament with no fracture, in a patient on an anticoagulant, which raises his bleeding risk. For the plan, I am stopping the ibuprofen because of the bleeding risk with apixaban. I am increasing acetaminophen from 500 mg as needed to 1000 mg every 8 hours for the next week, not to exceed 3 g per day. He will continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily without interruption. He gets a lace-up ankle brace and crutches for a few days, with weight bearing as tolerated, and he will use rest, ice, compression, and elevation. note:
Doctor: Hi, what brings you in today?
Patient: My eyes are red and gooey. It started in my left eye three days ago and now the right one is doing it too. I wake up with them stuck shut.
Doctor: I see. So we are seeing a 47-year-old male with red, sticky eyes. Is there any pain, or any change in your vision?
Patient: They feel gritty and itchy, but no real pain. My vision is fine, maybe a little blurry until I wipe the gunk away.
Doctor: Any sensitivity to light? Any injury, or anything that got into the eye?
Patient: No sensitivity to light, no injury. I do not wear contacts.
Doctor: Is anyone around you sick with pink eye?
Patient: A coworker had it last week.
Doctor: Any cold symptoms, ear pain, or sore throat?
Patient: I have had a stuffy nose and a mild sore throat for a few days. No ear pain, no fever.
Doctor: Do you have any medical conditions, and what do you take?
Patient: High blood pressure. I take amlodipine 5 mg once a day. Nothing else.
Doctor: Any allergies to medications?
Patient: Yes, I am allergic to sulfa drugs. I got a bad rash and hives from a sulfa antibiotic years ago.
Doctor: Thank you, that matters, because some common eye drops contain sulfa, so I will avoid those. Your temperature is 98.4, blood pressure 128/80, and heart rate 76. Your visual acuity is 20/20 in both eyes. Both eyes show redness of the white part with yellow-green mucus discharge and crusting of the lashes. The corneas are clear, and the fluorescein stain shows no ulcer or scratch. Your pupils are equal and react normally. I do not feel any swollen glands in front of your ears. Your ears look normal, your nose is congested, and your throat is mildly red without pus.
Patient: Is it bacterial or viral?
Doctor: With this much thick discharge, it looks like bacterial conjunctivitis, though your cold symptoms mean a virus could be playing a part. I will treat it as bacterial. I am prescribing moxifloxacin eye drops, one drop in both eyes three times daily for 7 days. You can use artificial tears as needed for the gritty feeling. Keep taking your amlodipine. Wash your hands often, do not share towels, and change your pillowcase daily. You can return to work 24 hours after starting the drops. Come back or see an eye doctor if you have eye pain, light sensitivity, worsening vision, or no improvement in 3 days.
Patient: Okay, thank you.
summary: A 47-year-old male presented with three days of red, itchy, gritty eyes with sticky discharge, starting in the left eye and spreading to the right, along with a stuffy nose and mild sore throat. He denies eye pain, light sensitivity, injury, ear pain, and fever, and has a sulfa drug allergy causing rash and hives. Visual acuity was 20/20, with mucopurulent discharge and clear corneas on fluorescein stain. The assessment was bacterial conjunctivitis. He was prescribed moxifloxacin eye drops for 7 days, artificial tears as needed, hygiene advice, and return precautions.
